summary.text: Bauxite is a sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content, and it is the world's main source of aluminium and gallium.
It is usually strip mined because it is almost always found near the surface, with little or no overburden.
Most of it is processed first into alumina and then into aluminium by electrolysis, after hot sodium hydroxide dissolves the aluminium in the Bayer process.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Les Baux, a village in southern France

facts.label: Largest producer
facts.value: Guinea, followed by Australia and China

facts.label: Typical depth
facts.value: Mostly within 1 to 20 metres of the surface

items.prompt: Before the Hall–Héroult process, early pure aluminium cost more than gold. Why was it so expensive?

options.label: Refining was complicated and used costly materials
Bauxite deposits had not yet been found anywhere
Aluminium could only be taken from meteorites
Governments heavily taxed every ounce produced

items.explain: Ore was refined by heating it with sodium or potassium in a vacuum, a complicated method using materials that were expensive at the time.

items.prompt: A ship is carrying a hold full of very damp bauxite. What is the main danger at sea?

options.label: The cargo can catch fire on its own
It gives off toxic fumes in the hold
It can turn fluid, shift and tip the ship
It swells and cracks the hull open

items.explain: Excessively moist bauxite may liquefy, letting the cargo shift rapidly and make the ship unstable, potentially sinking it.

items.prompt: Compared with making aluminium from ore, what does recycling aluminium need less of?

options.label: Sodium hydroxide only
Electric power
Workers on site
Shipping by sea

items.explain: Recycling requires less electric power than producing aluminium from ores, which could considerably extend bauxite reserves.

items.prompt: Bauxite is often dug out of wide, shallow pits instead of deep tunnels. Why?

options.label: Tunnels would collapse in such soft rock
Deep bauxite is too poor in aluminium
Laws forbid underground bauxite mines
It lies near the surface with little cover

items.explain: Bauxite is almost always found near the surface with little or no overburden, so strip mining is the usual method.

items.prompt: Granite is weathering into lateritic bauxite. Which conditions does that most depend on?

options.label: Cold weather and frozen ground
Intense weathering and very good drainage
Deep burial and high pressure
Still water with poor drainage

items.explain: Bauxite formation depends on intense weathering in a well-drained spot, which dissolves kaolinite and lets gibbsite precipitate.

items.prompt: In a can test, a sample of bauxite cargo is struck many times and stays dry. What does that prove?

options.label: The cargo is certified safe to load
The cargo will never liquefy
The cargo is too dry to sell
Nothing conclusive about its safety

items.explain: A slurry signals a risk of liquefying, but a dry sample does not conclusively prove the cargo will stay dry or is safe to load.
